summary: Describes how a DNS recursive resolver can run a copy of the root zone locally. This cuts round-trip times to root servers and prevents third parties from watching the queries sent to them.

plainLanguage.summary: A recursive resolver can keep a copy of the DNS root zone on its own host. It must validate and refresh that copy, and stop using it if it becomes stale.

subtitle: How a recursive resolver can serve a local copy of the DNS root zone.

tldr.problem: Some recursive resolvers have long or unreliable paths to root servers, and operators may want to keep root queries from being visible on those paths.
tldr.mechanism: The resolver uses an up-to-date copy of the full root zone on the same host, validates responses with DNSSEC, and refreshes the copy using its SOA timers.
tldr.outcome: The RFC requires the local service to answer only the same host and requires a switch to remote root servers if the local copy expires. It obsoletes RFC 7706.

today: RFC 8806 is an Informational RFC published in June 2020 that obsoletes RFC 7706. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Serve the Root Zone Locally
sections.content:
A recursive resolver may need to ask a root server about a top-level domain that is not in its cache. A local root-zone copy can reduce those requests' round-trip time and keep them off the network between the resolver and remote root servers.

The RFC says this method can add operational fragility: a broken local service can return bad data or make name resolution fail in ways that are hard to diagnose. It does not promise faster answers for names whose top-level-domain records are already cached.
sections.plainLanguage: A local root-zone copy can help when remote root-server access is slow or exposed to observation. The operator must manage the extra local service carefully.

sections.title: Requirements for the Local Copy
sections.content:
The system must validate signed zone records with DNSSEC, keep an up-to-date copy of the public root Key Signing Key, and retrieve the full root zone including DNSSEC records. An authoritative service for the root zone must run on the same host as the resolver and answer only that host.

The local authoritative data must match the public root zone. The RFC says glue records should not be changed because changes could cause problems for the resolver.
sections.plainLanguage: The resolver must verify the root-zone data and use a full, current copy. The local service must not answer queries from other hosts.

sections.title: Refreshing and Falling Back
sections.content:
The operator retrieves the zone and starts a local service that only the resolver on the same host can reach. The zone must be refreshed using the timers in its Start of Authority (SOA) record, so the local copy may briefly lag behind remote root servers.

The resolver must not serve stale root-zone data. If the copy cannot be refreshed before the SOA expire time, it must immediately switch to non-local root servers. The RFC recommends an automated check that confirms the copy is being refreshed.
sections.plainLanguage: Refresh the root-zone copy using its SOA timers and monitor that refresh. If the copy expires before an update arrives, use remote root servers instead.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 7706
sections.content:
RFC 7706 required the root server instance to use the loopback interface. RFC 8806 allows another local service, as long as only the resolver on that same host can query it.

The revision also removes a prohibition on distributing resolver software with this configuration, describes fallback to remote root servers when the local service fails, and updates source and configuration examples.
sections.plainLanguage: The revised guidance allows different ways to run the local service. It keeps the same-host restriction and adds a requirement to fall back when the local copy cannot be used.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Without DNSSEC validation, a local root-zone copy can be altered and cause bad responses, just as an unvalidated remote response can. Operators should understand the operational benefits and costs of DNSSEC.

Limiting queries to resolvers on the same host also limits the impact if the local root data is altered. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC validation helps detect altered root data. Keeping the service local limits which resolvers can be affected by a bad copy.
